# In Geneva, the World Can Anchor AI Governance in Free Expression

*Broken Chair* or *Chaise Cassee* is a wooden sculpture by the Swiss artist Daniel Berset and Louis Geneve outside the United Nations in Geneva, Switzerland. [Shutterstock](https://www.shutterstock.com/image-photo/geneva-switzerland-july-20-2019-broken-1964699488?trackingId=a51ec6f0-efb9-40fb-9f82-7b023856f2be&listId=searchResults)

The United Nations is convening its [Global Dialogue on Artificial Intelligence Governance](https://www.un.org/global-dialogue-ai-governance/en) in Geneva July 6-7, and the stakes are high: what rights will anchor the future of how the world governs AI? Generative AI systems mediate, filter, and generate the information we encounter every day. They are, at their core, a technology of expression and access to information. How we govern them will have downstream effects on what people can say, seek, and know. Geneva is where we can get that right.

## **A foundation worth building on**

The past several years produced exceptional progress on examining the interactions between generative AI and rights. The [Paris AI Action Summit](https://www.elysee.fr/en/sommet-pour-l-action-sur-l-ia) in February 2025 produced a declaration signed by 58 sovereign states that anchored AI governance in human rights and sustainability. Notably, the [US and UK declined](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2025/feb/11/us-uk-paris-ai-summit-artificial-intelligence-declaration) to join — a fracture in rights-focused alignment by AI powerhouses that contributes to the urgency in Geneva.

Despite that setback, this rights-centered commitment was reinforced months later at the regional organizational level. In October 2025, the UN Special Rapporteur on freedom of expression, alongside counterparts from the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), the Organization of American States (OAS), and the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR), [issued a joint declaration](https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/documents/issues/expression/statements/2025-10-24-joint-declaration-artificial-intelligence.pdf) affirming that freedom of expression must be embedded throughout the AI lifecycle, from design and training to deployment.

These expert-level commitments reflected obligations towards freedom of expression and access to information UN Member States had already adopted by consensus in 2024 through the Global Digital Compact. The Compact committed governments to protecting freedom of expression and access to information when mitigating potential harms and to refrain from information restrictions inconsistent with international law, a meaningful commitment in a universal instrument. It was the Global Digital Compact that established the upcoming Global Dialogue on AI Governance. Even the earliest intergovernmental standard on AI had already embedded this logic, and the [2024 revision to the OECD AI Principles](https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/en/instruments/oecd-legal-0449) conditioned information integrity measures on respect for freedom of expression.

Together, these instruments establish a baseline that governments have already agreed to. Geneva can build on and strengthen this baseline, ensuring that free expression and access to information are robustly protected in the AI era.

## **The New Delhi Declaration: an opportunity not taken**

This year’s [India AI Impact Summit](https://impact.indiaai.gov.in/) was a missed opportunity for human rights and, in particular, freedom of expression. The international community fell short of building AI governance on a human rights foundation. The [New Delhi Declaration](https://www.newsonair.gov.in/india-ai-impact-summit-2026-adopts-new-delhi-declaration), endorsed by more than 90 countries and international organizations, called for “industry-led voluntary measures” and described AI’s purpose as advancing “social good,” without accountability mechanisms or rights standards attached to that phrase.

Before the summit, [a keyword analysis of its agenda](https://www.techpolicy.press/indias-ai-impact-summit-promises-little-more-than-spectacle/) found “innovation,” “growth,” “efficiency,” and “productivity” dominating the program, while “human rights,” “accountability,” and “surveillance” were largely absent from high-level plenary titles.

The Dialogue's human rights cluster and its independent scientific panel provide the structural anchors that the last summit’s voluntary framework deliberately avoided. This gives Geneva the opportunity to correct what was left behind in New Delhi by reaffirming the integral role of human rights in AI governance.

## **Why freedom of expression Is central to AI**

Generative AI systems now reach over a billion people globally, and information-seeking [became the leading use-case](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/generative-ai-and-news-report-2025-how-people-think-about-ais-role-journalism-and-society) of generative AI in 2025 across six countries (Argentina, Denmark, France, Japan, the UK, and the US). Whether or not you directly use a chatbot, you likely receive an AI-generated summary every time you search online through services like Google AI Overviews or Bing Copilot Search. That reach makes AI governance inseparable from the governance of expression itself.

International human rights law [provides a solid basis](https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/731540?ln=en&v=pdf) on which to build AI governance in the new era. Article 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the main instrument protecting freedom of expression globally, [protects the right](https://www.un.org/en/about-us/universal-declaration-of-human-rights) to “seek, receive and impart information and ideas […] regardless of frontiers” through any media. This forward-looking wording provides a solid basis to protect AI-generated expression and information that the international community can rely on.

Article 19 should be top of mind to all those participating in the Global Dialogue this summer. Governments have often invoked information accuracy and public order to restrict sociopolitical expression online, endangering political speech, government criticism, journalism, and advocacy. While information integrity is a genuine concern, there is a danger in invoking it without the necessary counterbalance of Article 19's strict requirements in AI governance. This tripartite test [dictates that](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no34-article-19-freedoms-opinion-and) any restriction must be provided for in law, pursue a legitimate aim, and be necessary to protect a legitimate aim.

#### Our content delivered to your inbox.

#### Thank you!

Article 19 is also a helpful tool because it enables policymakers to tackle real harms, like non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material, while protecting the tenets of democracy.

## **Why rights protections matter in practice**

Over the last three years, it has become clear that the importance of protecting freedom of expression and access to information extends beyond theory. The examples of free speech abuses under vague safety arguments have been too numerous.

In India, when Google’s Gemini [generated responses in February 2024](https://www.techpolicy.press/the-many-questions-about-indias-new-ai-advisory/) describing the prime minister’s policies in terms some experts characterized as fascist, the government accused Google of violating IT Rules and issued a formal advisory requiring pre-clearance for AI model launches. The message to AI developers was unmistakable: outputs that displease the government create legal exposure. India’s [three-hour removal rule for AI-generated content](https://dig.watch/updates/india-enforces-a-three-hour-removal-rule-for-ai-generated-deepfake-content), introduced in early 2026, compounded that pressure. Platforms must now remove flagged unlawful content within three hours of a government notification. The rule draws no distinction between political satire, journalism, and genuinely harmful material, and it reaches political opponents, journalists, ordinary users, and civil society organizations alike. India’s [digital censorship infrastructure](https://www.techpolicy.press/three-justifications-and-the-ai-accelerant-of-indias-digital-censorship-infrastructure/) saw direct content blocking orders more than double to over 24,000 in 2025. The AI removal rule extends that infrastructure into a new medium. However, the use of public order as grounds for restricting AI outputs is not unique to India.

In Turkey, a [court blocked access](https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/turkey-blocks-xs-grok-chatbot-alleged-insults-erdogan-2025-07-09/) to Grok content in July 2025 after the xAI chatbot generated outputs deemed insulting to President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. The stated rationale was to protect public order, precisely the kind of rationale that Article 19’s proportionality requirements exist to constrain.

These pressures are not confined to governments with established records of censorship. In the US, [domestic debates over neutrality](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/07/preventing-woke-ai-in-the-federal-government/) in AI have complicated a principled international stance on freedom of expression. The European Union’s [AI Act](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/) and [Digital Services Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/digital-services-act) contain systemic risk provisions broad enough to function as speech restrictions, with national regulators already [criticizing chatbots](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/oct/21/ai-chatbots-unreliable-biased-advice-voters-dutch-watchdog) for producing “biased” political outputs, which is a pattern worth keeping an eye on.

Most consequentially for Geneva, China's approach is not merely domestic. In July of last year, China released its [Global AI Governance Action Plan](https://www.fmprc.gov.cn/mfa_eng/xw/zyxw/202507/t20250729_11679232.html), invoking “public good” and “safety” as governing principles. Unsurprisingly, China’s domestic AI regime requires adherence to [“core socialist values”](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/china-s-ai-governance-ambitions-and-their-implications-for-free-expression) and restricts outputs that may challenge state authority or social order. This framework is being actively promoted in the same multilateral forums whose outcomes will determine whether freedom of expression is protected in global AI governance.

## **What the Global Dialogue can achieve**

The [UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI](https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000380455) of 2021 provides a template on what rights-based AI governance can look like, providing inspiration for what the results of the Global Dialogue may look like. The UNESCO Recommendation requires any limitation on rights to follow the tripartite test (legality, legitimacy, and proportionality), bars AI systems from being used for social scoring or mass surveillance, and requires member states to ensure that AI actors respect rights in the AI lifecycle. This represents a model worth returning to. Building on its foundation, the Global Dialogue can go further: holding freedom of expression and access to information as an operative standard and applying the Article 19 tripartite test for AI content governance.

The [Global Dialogue’s](https://www.un.org/global-dialogue-ai-governance/en) human rights cluster and the Independent International Scientific Panel can operationalize commitments that UN Member States have already made. As we argued in our [submission to the Global Dialogue’s call for input](https://www.bedrockprinciple.com/p/why-free-expression-must-anchor-global), we propose:

- The Co-Chairs' Summary and any working group mandates adopted at Geneva should name freedom of expression and access to information explicitly — closely following the Global Digital Compact's commitments — with civil society and independent experts participating substantively in the process.
- The Scientific Panel should assess the latest capabilities of AI-enabled surveillance and content authenticity technology in order to fully assess the potential harms to freedom of expression, alongside privacy.
- The Dialogue should affirm that Article 19’s requirements of legality, legitimacy, and necessity are consistently held throughout the conversation around AI governance, particularly regarding information integrity measures and any speech restrictions.

AI is the information technology of the future, and it deserves governance that gives careful consideration to rights protection. Geneva is where rights-respecting best practices can be made global, breaching national and regional divides.

# 在日內瓦，世界可以讓言論自由成為 AI 治理的基石

*Broken Chair* 或 *Chaise Cassee* 是瑞士藝術家 Daniel Berset 與 Louis Geneve 創作的木製雕塑，位於瑞士日內瓦的聯合國外。[Shutterstock](https://www.shutterstock.com/image-photo/geneva-switzerland-july-20-2019-broken-1964699488?trackingId=a51ec6f0-efb9-40fb-9f82-7b023856f2be&listId=searchResults)

聯合國將於 7 月 6 至 7 日在日內瓦召開[全球人工智慧治理對話](https://www.un.org/global-dialogue-ai-governance/en)，而此事攸關重大：哪些權利將成為未來全球治理 AI 的基礎？生成式 AI 系統中介、篩選並生成我們每天接觸的資訊。它們的核心，是一種關乎表達與資訊近用的技術。我們如何治理它們，將對人們能說什麼、尋求什麼、知道什麼產生後續影響。日內瓦正是我們可以把這件事做對的地方。

## **值得據以建構的基礎**

過去幾年，在檢視生成式 AI 與權利之間的互動方面，已有非凡進展。2025 年 2 月的[巴黎 AI 行動峰會](https://www.elysee.fr/en/sommet-pour-l-action-sur-l-ia)產出了一份由 58 個主權國家簽署的宣言，將 AI 治理奠基於人權與永續性。值得注意的是，[美國與英國拒絕加入](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2025/feb/11/us-uk-paris-ai-summit-artificial-intelligence-declaration)；這顯示 AI 強權之間以權利為核心的協調出現裂痕，也使日內瓦的討論更顯迫切。

儘管遭遇這項挫折，這項以權利為中心的承諾，數月後在區域組織層級獲得強化。2025 年 10 月，聯合國言論自由特別報告員，與歐洲安全與合作組織（OSCE）、美洲國家組織（OAS）及非洲人權和民族權委員會（ACHPR）的相對職位代表，共同[發布聯合宣言](https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/documents/issues/expression/statements/2025-10-24-joint-declaration-artificial-intelligence.pdf)，確認言論自由必須貫穿 AI 生命週期的各個環節，從設計、訓練到部署皆然。

這些專家層級的承諾，反映了聯合國會員國在 2024 年已透過《全球數位契約》以共識通過、對言論自由與資訊近用所承擔的義務。該契約承諾各國政府在減輕潛在危害時保護言論自由與資訊近用，並避免採取不符合國際法的資訊限制；在一項普遍性文書中，這是相當有意義的承諾。也正是《全球數位契約》設立了即將展開的全球 AI 治理對話。即使是最早期的政府間 AI 標準，也已經把這套邏輯納入其中，而 [2024 年修訂的 OECD AI 原則](https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/en/instruments/oecd-legal-0449)則將資訊完整性措施建立在尊重言論自由的前提上。

整體而言，這些文書建立了一條各國政府已經同意的基準。日內瓦可以在這個基準上繼續推進並加以強化，確保言論自由與資訊近用在 AI 時代受到堅實保護。

## **《新德里宣言》：未被把握的機會**

今年的[印度 AI 影響力峰會](https://impact.indiaai.gov.in/)錯失了人權，尤其是言論自由方面的機會。國際社會未能把 AI 治理建立在人權基礎之上。獲得 90 多個國家與國際組織背書的[《新德里宣言》](https://www.newsonair.gov.in/india-ai-impact-summit-2026-adopts-new-delhi-declaration)呼籲採取「由產業主導的自願性措施」，並將 AI 的目的描述為促進「社會公益」，卻沒有為這個說法附上問責機制或權利標準。

峰會之前，[一項針對其議程的關鍵字分析](https://www.techpolicy.press/indias-ai-impact-summit-promises-little-more-than-spectacle/)發現，「創新」、「成長」、「效率」與「生產力」主導了整個議程，而「人權」、「問責」與「監控」則大多未出現在高階全體會議的標題中。

這場對話的人權群組與獨立科學小組，提供了上屆峰會的自願性框架刻意迴避的結構性支柱。這讓日內瓦有機會重新確認人權在 AI 治理中的整體性角色，補上新德里留下的缺口。

## **為什麼表意自由是 AI 的核心**

生成式 AI 系統如今觸及全球超過十億人，而在 2025 年，資訊搜尋[成為生成式 AI 的主要使用情境](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/generative-ai-and-news-report-2025-how-people-think-about-ais-role-journalism-and-society)，橫跨六個國家（阿根廷、丹麥、法國、日本、英國與美國）。不論你是否直接使用聊天機器人，每當你透過 Google AI Overviews 或 Bing Copilot Search 等服務上網搜尋時，很可能都會收到 AI 生成的摘要。這樣的觸及範圍，使 AI 治理與表意本身的治理密不可分。

國際人權法[提供了堅實基礎](https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/731540?ln=en&v=pdf)，可用來建立新時代的 AI 治理。全球保障表意自由的主要工具《公民與政治權利國際公約》第 19 條，[保障人們](https://www.un.org/en/about-us/universal-declaration-of-human-rights)透過任何媒介「尋求、接收和傳遞資訊與思想［……］不受國界限制」的權利。這種具前瞻性的措辭，為保護 AI 生成的表意與資訊提供了國際社會可以依據的堅實基礎。

今年夏天參與全球對話的所有人，都應該把第 19 條放在優先位置。各國政府常以資訊正確性與公共秩序為由，限制線上的社會政治表意，危及政治言論、對政府的批評、新聞工作與倡議。資訊完整性確實是值得關注的問題，但若在 AI 治理中引用這個概念時，沒有同時以第 19 條的嚴格要求作為必要制衡，就會產生危險。這項三段式檢驗[要求](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no34-article-19-freedoms-opinion-and)，任何限制都必須由法律明文規定、追求正當目的，且是保護該正當目的所必要的手段。

#### 我們的內容直接寄到你的收件匣。

#### 謝謝！

第 19 條也是一項有用的工具，因為它讓政策制定者能夠處理真實傷害，例如未經同意的私密影像與兒童性虐待內容，同時保護民主的基本原則。

## **為什麼權利保障在實務上很重要**

過去三年來，保護言論自由與資訊取得的重要性，已經很明顯不只是理論問題。以模糊的安全理由濫用言論限制的例子，實在太多了。

在印度，Google 的 Gemini 於 2024 年 2 月[生成回應](https://www.techpolicy.press/the-many-questions-about-indias-new-ai-advisory/)，用一些專家形容為法西斯的字眼描述總理的政策後，政府指控 Google 違反 IT Rules（資訊科技規則），並發布正式指引，要求 AI 模型發布前必須事先核准。這傳達給 AI 開發者的訊息再清楚不過：讓政府不悅的輸出內容，會帶來法律風險。印度在 2026 年初推出的 [AI 生成內容三小時移除規則](https://dig.watch/updates/india-enforces-a-three-hour-removal-rule-for-ai-generated-deepfake-content)，進一步加重了這種壓力。平台如今必須在收到政府通知後三小時內，移除被標記為違法的內容。這項規則沒有區分政治諷刺、新聞報導與真正有害的內容，也同樣波及政治反對者、記者、一般使用者與公民社會組織。印度的[數位審查基礎設施](https://www.techpolicy.press/three-justifications-and-the-ai-accelerant-of-indias-digital-censorship-infrastructure/)在 2025 年直接封鎖內容的命令增加超過一倍，超過 24,000 件。AI 移除規則把這套基礎設施延伸到新的媒介。不過，以公共秩序作為限制 AI 輸出內容的理由，並不是印度獨有的現象。

在土耳其，2025 年 7 月，xAI 聊天機器人生成被認定侮辱總統雷傑普・塔伊普・艾爾段（Recep Tayyip Erdoğan）的輸出內容後，法院[封鎖了](https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/turkey-blocks-xs-grok-chatbot-alleged-insults-erdogan-2025-07-09/)對 Grok 內容的存取。官方提出的理由是保護公共秩序，而這正是第 19 條的比例原則要求所要限制的那類理由。

這些壓力並不限於已有審查紀錄的政府。在美國，[國內對 AI 中立性的辯論](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/07/preventing-woke-ai-in-the-federal-government/)讓美國在言論自由上的原則性國際立場變得更加複雜。歐盟的 [AI Act](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/) 與 [Digital Services Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/digital-services-act) 都包含範圍相當廣的系統性風險條款，足以被用作言論限制；各國監管機關也已經開始[批評聊天機器人](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/oct/21/ai-chatbots-unreliable-biased-advice-voters-dutch-watchdog)產出「有偏見」的政治內容，這是一種值得持續留意的模式。

對日內瓦而言，影響最深遠的是，中國的做法並不只是國內政策。去年 7 月，中國發布了[《全球人工智慧治理行動計畫》](https://www.fmprc.gov.cn/mfa_eng/xw/zyxw/202507/t20250729_11679232.html)，以「公共善」與「安全」作為治理原則。毫不意外地，中國國內的 AI 制度要求遵守[「社會主義核心價值觀」](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/china-s-ai-governance-ambitions-and-their-implications-for-free-expression)，並限制可能挑戰國家權威或社會秩序的輸出。這套框架正被積極推廣到同樣的多邊論壇中，而這些論壇的成果將決定全球 AI 治理是否會保護言論自由。

## **全球對話能達成什麼**

2021 年的 [UNESCO《人工智慧倫理建議書》](https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000380455)，提供了一個以權利為本的 AI 治理可能樣貌，也為全球對話可能產出的成果提供參考。這份 UNESCO 建議書要求，任何對權利的限制都必須符合三階段檢驗（合法性、正當性與比例性）；禁止將 AI 系統用於社會評分或大規模監控；並要求會員國確保 AI 相關行為者在 AI 生命週期中尊重權利。這是一個值得回頭借鏡的模式。在此基礎上，全球對話可以更進一步：把言論自由與取得資訊的權利作為可操作的標準，並將《第 19 條》的三階段檢驗適用於 AI 內容治理。

[全球對話](https://www.un.org/global-dialogue-ai-governance/en)的人權議題群組與獨立國際科學小組，可以將聯合國會員國已經作出的承諾落實為具體操作。正如我們在[回應全球對話徵求意見的投稿](https://www.bedrockprinciple.com/p/why-free-expression-must-anchor-global)中所主張，我們提出：

- 在日內瓦通過的共同主席摘要，以及任何工作小組授權中，都應明確列出言論自由與取得資訊的權利，並緊扣《全球數位契約》的承諾；同時，公民社會與獨立專家也應實質參與整個過程。
- 科學小組應評估 AI 賦能監控與內容真實性技術的最新能力，以便在隱私之外，也能完整評估其對言論自由可能造成的傷害。
- 對話應確認，《第 19 條》對合法性、正當性與必要性的要求，必須在 AI 治理討論中持續貫徹，特別是在資訊完整性措施與任何言論限制方面。

AI 是未來的資訊技術，因此需要一套審慎考量權利保障的治理方式。日內瓦可以成為尊重權利的最佳實務走向全球之處，跨越國家與區域之間的分歧。

*Broken Chair* 或 *Chaise Cassee* 是瑞士藝術家 Daniel Berset 與 Louis Geneve 創作的木製雕塑，位於瑞士日內瓦的聯合國外。[Shutterstock](https://www.shutterstock.com/image-photo/geneva-switzerland-july-20-2019-broken-1964699488?trackingId=a51ec6f0-efb9-40fb-9f82-7b023856f2be&listId=searchResults)

聯合國將於 7 月 6 至 7 日在日內瓦召開[全球人工智慧治理對話](https://www.un.org/global-dialogue-ai-governance/en)，而此事攸關重大：哪些權利將成為未來全球治理 AI 的基礎？生成式 AI 系統中介、篩選並生成我們每天接觸的資訊。它們的核心，是一種關乎表達與資訊近用的技術。我們如何治理它們，將對人們能說什麼、尋求什麼、知道什麼產生後續影響。日內瓦正是我們可以把這件事做對的地方。

過去幾年，在檢視生成式 AI 與權利之間的互動方面，已有非凡進展。2025 年 2 月的[巴黎 AI 行動峰會](https://www.elysee.fr/en/sommet-pour-l-action-sur-l-ia)產出了一份由 58 個主權國家簽署的宣言，將 AI 治理奠基於人權與永續性。值得注意的是，[美國與英國拒絕加入](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2025/feb/11/us-uk-paris-ai-summit-artificial-intelligence-declaration)；這顯示 AI 強權之間以權利為核心的協調出現裂痕，也使日內瓦的討論更顯迫切。

儘管遭遇這項挫折，這項以權利為中心的承諾，數月後在區域組織層級獲得強化。2025 年 10 月，聯合國言論自由特別報告員，與歐洲安全與合作組織（OSCE）、美洲國家組織（OAS）及非洲人權和民族權委員會（ACHPR）的相對職位代表，共同[發布聯合宣言](https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/documents/issues/expression/statements/2025-10-24-joint-declaration-artificial-intelligence.pdf)，確認言論自由必須貫穿 AI 生命週期的各個環節，從設計、訓練到部署皆然。

這些專家層級的承諾，反映了聯合國會員國在 2024 年已透過《全球數位契約》以共識通過、對言論自由與資訊近用所承擔的義務。該契約承諾各國政府在減輕潛在危害時保護言論自由與資訊近用，並避免採取不符合國際法的資訊限制；在一項普遍性文書中，這是相當有意義的承諾。也正是《全球數位契約》設立了即將展開的全球 AI 治理對話。即使是最早期的政府間 AI 標準，也已經把這套邏輯納入其中，而 [2024 年修訂的 OECD AI 原則](https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/en/instruments/oecd-legal-0449)則將資訊完整性措施建立在尊重言論自由的前提上。

整體而言，這些文書建立了一條各國政府已經同意的基準。日內瓦可以在這個基準上繼續推進並加以強化，確保言論自由與資訊近用在 AI 時代受到堅實保護。

## **《新德里宣言》：未被把握的機會**

今年的[印度 AI 影響力峰會](https://impact.indiaai.gov.in/)錯失了人權，尤其是言論自由方面的機會。國際社會未能把 AI 治理建立在人權基礎之上。獲得 90 多個國家與國際組織背書的[《新德里宣言》](https://www.newsonair.gov.in/india-ai-impact-summit-2026-adopts-new-delhi-declaration)呼籲採取「由產業主導的自願性措施」，並將 AI 的目的描述為促進「社會公益」，卻沒有為這個說法附上問責機制或權利標準。

峰會之前，[一項針對其議程的關鍵字分析](https://www.techpolicy.press/indias-ai-impact-summit-promises-little-more-than-spectacle/)發現，「創新」、「成長」、「效率」與「生產力」主導了整個議程，而「人權」、「問責」與「監控」則大多未出現在高階全體會議的標題中。

這場對話的人權群組與獨立科學小組，提供了上屆峰會的自願性框架刻意迴避的結構性支柱。這讓日內瓦有機會重新確認人權在 AI 治理中的整體性角色，補上新德里留下的缺口。

## **為什麼表意自由是 AI 的核心**

生成式 AI 系統如今觸及全球超過十億人，而在 2025 年，資訊搜尋[成為生成式 AI 的主要使用情境](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/generative-ai-and-news-report-2025-how-people-think-about-ais-role-journalism-and-society)，橫跨六個國家（阿根廷、丹麥、法國、日本、英國與美國）。不論你是否直接使用聊天機器人，每當你透過 Google AI Overviews 或 Bing Copilot Search 等服務上網搜尋時，很可能都會收到 AI 生成的摘要。這樣的觸及範圍，使 AI 治理與表意本身的治理密不可分。

國際人權法[提供了堅實基礎](https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/731540?ln=en&v=pdf)，可用來建立新時代的 AI 治理。全球保障表意自由的主要工具《公民與政治權利國際公約》第 19 條，[保障人們](https://www.un.org/en/about-us/universal-declaration-of-human-rights)透過任何媒介「尋求、接收和傳遞資訊與思想［……］不受國界限制」的權利。這種具前瞻性的措辭，為保護 AI 生成的表意與資訊提供了國際社會可以依據的堅實基礎。

今年夏天參與全球對話的所有人，都應該把第 19 條放在優先位置。各國政府常以資訊正確性與公共秩序為由，限制線上的社會政治表意，危及政治言論、對政府的批評、新聞工作與倡議。資訊完整性確實是值得關注的問題，但若在 AI 治理中引用這個概念時，沒有同時以第 19 條的嚴格要求作為必要制衡，就會產生危險。這項三段式檢驗[要求](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no34-article-19-freedoms-opinion-and)，任何限制都必須由法律明文規定、追求正當目的，且是保護該正當目的所必要的手段。
